source.title: When Scaling Meets LLM Finetuning: The Effect of Data, Model and Finetuning Method
source.authors: Biao Zhang; Zhongtao Liu; Colin Cherry; Orhan Firat

record.tranche_reason: The study tests scaling in fine-tuning and refines its scope, reporting task- and method-dependent exponents, weak PET-parameter scaling, and a notable 16B extrapolation mismatch.
record.gate_note: The study does not test fixed-compute optimal allocation or architecture-shape sensitivity. Its main scaling results concern test-set perplexity after fine-tuning, rather than held-out pretraining loss. It also reports a held-out pretraining-PPL size sweep in Figure 10. Cited findings from other work are not recorded as results. Some downstream scaling and zero-shot results are presented only in figures; figure-only results are identified below.
record.test_reason: The study fits power laws to fine-tuning test PPL across model size (1B–16B), pretraining tokens, PET parameters and fine-tuning data, with held-out errors. This is a new setting (LLM fine-tuning) with direct results on V5. A small pretraining size sweep (Fig. 10) also bears on V1, V2 and V7. It is mainly an extension, not a refutation, so T3 fits better than T5.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add that the authors find the optimal fine-tuning method is task- and data-dependent, with critical data sizes varying greatly across tasks. They also find PET preserves zero-shot and few-shot generalization better than FMT. They frame the law as empirical, limited to closed generation tasks.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures downstream test PPL after supervised fine-tuning of bilingual models, rather than held-out pretraining loss or compute-optimal pretraining allocation; it also compares a multiplicative joint fit with an additive fit.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by downstream task, fine-tuning method, and scaling factor. The authors report prompt-tuning instability, noisy empirical points associated with unstable optimization and dev-set overfitting, and a 16B En-Zh pretraining instability that affects extrapolation.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning on one language pair can raise zero-shot translation into the same target language. Prompt and LoRA generalize better than FMT, especially with large base models (Fig. 6, figure only).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Effect of fine-tuning method and scale on zero-shot generalization to related tasks

fits_no_version.finding: FMT degrades few-shot capability as fine-tuning data grows, while PET retains most of it (Figs 11–14, figure only).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning data scale trades off against retained few-shot ability, depending on method

fits_no_version.finding: Model-size exponent exceeds the pretraining-data exponent (αm > αp) in fine-tuning scaling across tasks (Table 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning benefits more from parameters than from pretraining tokens

record.problems: The study covers closed generation tasks and a limited number of bilingual model sets. It reports optimization instability and some imperfect Prompt/LoRA optimization and evaluation. The En-Zh 16B pretraining result is an acknowledged mismatch, and its proposed cause is instability. Pretraining-data scaling uses intermediate checkpoints as proxies. Most fine-grained curve points are figure-only; the text reports mean absolute deviations but no uncertainty intervals.
record.rows_left_out: No results omitted to meet the 60-row limit. Detailed single-variable fine-tuning-data plots (Figure 1), BLEURT/RougeL scaling curves (Figures 7–9), and few-shot plots (Figures 11–14) are not separately enumerated; the relevant reported fit errors and PPL-quality correlations are recorded in r3–r50.

untested.parts: Token and compute axes; only about 1.2 orders of magnitude in parameters (1B–16B); En-De fit quality not quantified.
Extrapolation across orders of magnitude; only a 2x extrapolation (8B to 16B) is examined.
Entirely untested; no fixed-compute allocation sweep.
Entirely untested; depth and width co-vary with size (Table 3).
Other modalities, repeated data, and transfer regimes other than supervised fine-tuning on translation and summarization.
Downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss; downstream-vs-scale curves (Figs 7–9) are figure-only.
Compute-optimal split, parameter-counting conventions (PET params omitted, said to make little difference), training schedule.

missing.what: Table 6 per-task averages: MLSum additive held-out error is lower than multiplicative for all three factors (0.013 vs 0.014, 0.005 vs 0.007, 0.004 vs 0.0055), contrary to the caption's 'overall' claim.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The 1B–16B range is narrow for V1 and V2, and only r2 gives a stated (textual) pretraining result; r1 is figure-only. Rows r3–r26 share β and E across factors because these were fitted jointly. The V6 rows link downstream metrics to fine-tuned task PPL, not to pretraining loss or scale directly.

versions.untested_parts: Tests parameter-count scaling of validation PPL for En-De and En-Zh LLM pretraining only; does not test token-count or compute scaling, or several orders of magnitude.
Tests a limited size extrapolation to 16B, not prediction across orders of magnitude; does not test token- or compute-based extrapolation.
No fixed-compute budget or loss-minimising parameter/token allocation sweep.
No controlled depth/width or architecture comparison at fixed parameter count.
Tests fine-tuning of bilingual language models on translation and summarization, not other modalities, repeated data, or other fine-tuning/transfer regimes.
Tests downstream translation and summarization measures in the reported settings; does not establish downstream predictability generally.

Tests variation by task, fine-tuning method, and fitting formulation, plus one reported unstable 16B extrapolation. Does not test compute-optimal-split dependence, parameter-count conventions, or a broad range of training schedules and fitting methods.
